explanation: The change-event log is the most storage-efficient design that preserves intraday point-in-time accuracy. Storage scales with actual change rate: at 2.5 changes per user per day on average, the change-event log produces rows proportional to actual user activity rather than a guaranteed full-state snapshot for every user every day. Users who rarely change preferences produce almost no rows. Point-in-time queries filter by changed_at ≤ event_timestamp and take the most recent value per (user_id, notification_type) — accurate to the second. Option B (deduplication of no-ops) is valid only if most of the 100–150M daily rows are phantom changes from the source system. The scenario states users genuinely toggle preferences 2–3 times per day — these are real changes, not no-ops. Removing real changes would incorrectly delete valid history. Option C (daily end-of-day snapshot) reduces storage to 18B rows/year and is much better than SCD Type 2, but caps accuracy at one day. If a user changes preferences at 10 AM and a click event occurs at 2 PM, the daily snapshot returns the prior end-of-day preference state — wrong for any intraday event analysis. The scenario explicitly requires second-level accuracy. Option D (SCD Type 1) destroys historical capability entirely and offloads the problem to the clickstream team.
hints: Storing a full preference state snapshot (12 types per row) on every change versus storing one row per individual change event — how does storage scale differently for a user who changes preferences rarely versus frequently?

A daily end-of-day snapshot has one row per user per day. If a user changes preferences at 10 AM and a click event occurs at 2 PM, does the daily snapshot return the correct preference state at event time?

title: Schema from Requirements: Naming the Fact Grain When Stakeholder Briefs Conflict
scenario_context: A subscription software company receives a stakeholder brief: 'We need analytics so Marketing can track acquisition campaigns by channel, and Finance can track monthly recurring revenue by product plan.' Marketing needs event-level data (one row per acquisition event) because their attribution model runs on individual events. Finance needs periodic snapshot data (one row per customer × product × month) because MRR is a balance metric computed at month-end. The data team must decide whether to build one fact table or two.
description: What is the correct design decision, and why does a single fact table fail to satisfy both stakeholders without sacrificing precision for one of them?
options: Build two separate facts: `fact_acquisition` at the acquisition-event level for Marketing and `fact_mrr_snapshot` at the customer × product × month level for Finance. An event-level fact and a periodic-snapshot fact have fundamentally different semantics; one table cannot serve both without losing either per-event attribution or the zero-activity period coverage Finance requires.

Use the acquisition-event level for a single fact table; add a month-end MRR column computed at load time so Finance can filter by month. Both stakeholders access one table, eliminating the need to maintain two separate facts.

Use the customer × product × month level for a single fact table; store acquisition event counts as a measure so Marketing can sum events per month. The periodic level is richer because it captures months with zero acquisitions.
Ask Marketing and Finance to align on a single level of detail before building; if they cannot agree, defer the project. Designing a fact table before agreement is reached is a governance violation.
explanation: Option A is correct. Transaction facts (event-level) and periodic snapshot facts (period-level) are different fact table types with different semantics. An event-level fact records something that happened; a periodic snapshot records state at the end of a period. A single table cannot satisfy both. Event-level MRR computation misses customers with active subscriptions but no acquisition events in a given month (subscription renewals without new-acquisition signals) — Finance's MRR would be understated. Period-level acquisition analysis loses individual event detail — Marketing cannot run per-event attribution models from a monthly aggregate. The correct design: two facts joined by conformed dimensions (dim_customer, dim_product, dim_date). Option B (add MRR column to event table) forces Finance to aggregate from events, missing zero-event active periods — incorrect MRR. Option C (period table with event counts) destroys per-event detail Marketing needs for attribution. Option D misframes the problem: two valid requirements that correspond to two standard fact table types is not a governance breakdown requiring stakeholder consensus — it is standard dimensional modeling practice.
hints: Marketing's attribution model runs on individual acquisition events; Finance's MRR is a balance metric measured at month-end. Are these two computational requirements compatible with a single level of detail without losing precision for one stakeholder?

A periodic snapshot fact includes one row for every period, even periods with zero activity. An event-level fact records only what happened. Which stakeholder's computation requires which type, and why?

title: Bridge Tables: Resolving a Many-to-Many Between Orders and Promotions
scenario_context: An e-commerce company runs multi-promotional campaigns: a single order can have multiple promotions applied (SUMMER10, LOYALTY5, NEWUSER20), and a single promotion applies to thousands of orders. The BI team needs to report: (1) revenue attributed to each promotion and (2) cross-promotion overlap (orders where two specific promotions coexisted). The current schema stores all applied promotion codes in a pipe-delimited varchar column `promo_codes` on the fact_orders table.
description: What is the correct dimensional design, and what specific analytical question does the pipe-delimited approach make impossible to answer in standard SQL?
options: Replace the pipe-delimited column with a `bridge_order_promotion` table (order_key, promotion_key, weight) — one row per order-promotion combination. Revenue attribution multiplies order revenue by weight per promotion row. Cross-promotion overlap is answered with a self-join on the bridge keyed by order_key. The bridge dissolves the many-to-many without repeating full revenue per promotion row.

Add up to five separate `promo_1_key` through `promo_5_key` foreign key columns to the fact table, each joining `dim_promotion` independently. This handles up to five simultaneous promotions per order without a separate bridge table.

Create a `fact_promotion_events` table with one row per promotion-order pair, storing the order's full revenue on each row. BI tools sum revenue grouped by promotion for attribution. The original fact_orders table retains the pipe-delimited column for backward compatibility.
Expand `dim_promotion` to include one row per unique combination of promotions that appear together on an order. Each fact row joins to its exact promotion-bundle row using a composite key.
explanation: Option A is correct. A bridge table stores one row per order-promotion pair with a weight column (e.g., 0.5 for two promotions equally weighted) so revenue is allocated across promotions without duplication. The pipe-delimited column fails on two counts: (1) SQL cannot GROUP BY individual promotion codes inside a delimited string using standard joins — revenue attribution requires string parsing that is not portable across BI tools; (2) cross-promotion overlap (`WHERE both SUMMER10 and LOYALTY5 applied`) cannot be expressed as a relational predicate on a varchar column. Option B (five key columns) breaks when a sixth promotion is added (schema change required), treats promotion slots as ordered positions with semantic meaning they lack, and produces NULLs for unused slots that must be coalesced in every query. Option C (separate fact with full revenue per row) double-counts: summing revenue across promotions gives N× for N-promotion orders. The weight column in the bridge prevents this double-count by design. Option D (combination dimension) explodes exponentially — with 10 active promotions and up to 5 per order, new combinations force new dimension rows and any change to the promotion catalog requires rebuilding the dimension.
hints: Can SQL's GROUP BY clause extract individual promotion codes from a pipe-delimited string without string-splitting functions? What does that limitation mean for building a promotion revenue report in a standard BI tool?

If a `fact_promotion_events` table stores the full order revenue on each promotion row and an order has two promotions, what is the sum of revenue across all rows for that order compared to the actual order revenue?

title: Denormalization Trade-offs: Flattening a Snowflake into a Star for a BI Workload
description: A dimensional model has a snowflaked product hierarchy: fact_sales → dim_product (product_key, subcategory_key) → dim_subcategory (subcategory_key, category_key) → dim_category (category_key, category_name). BI analysts complain that every drill-down query requires two intermediate joins, which slows BI tool query generation. The team debates flattening the snowflake into a single `dim_product` with subcategory_name and category_name inline. What is the correct trade-off analysis?
options: Flatten to a star: inline subcategory_name and category_name into `dim_product`. Query complexity drops from three joins to one and BI tool query generation simplifies. The cost is update anomalies: renaming a category requires updating all dim_product rows in that category, not just one dim_category row. This cost is acceptable when categories change rarely and an ETL manages updates consistently.

Keep the snowflake: normalization eliminates update anomalies and storage is more efficient in columnar warehouses because repeated category names compress better in a separate lookup table than duplicated across thousands of product rows.

Flatten to a star but enforce referential integrity via application-level ETL constraints: verify all rows sharing category_name have the same category_key before load. This gives query simplicity while maintaining the update-consistency guarantee of normalization.

Neither approach is correct; the proper solution is an OBT (one big table) embedding fact measures alongside all dimension attributes, which eliminates all joins and maximizes query performance beyond what star or snowflake schemas achieve.
explanation: Option A correctly identifies the trade-off. Flattening a snowflake into a star reduces query complexity (fewer joins) and typically improves query performance for BI workloads because modern columnar engines optimize wide dimension reads better than multi-hop normalized joins generated by BI tools. The explicit cost is update anomaly risk: when a category is renamed, all dim_product rows in that category must be updated instead of one dim_category row. This is acceptable when (1) category names change infrequently (quarterly product catalog updates, not daily), and (2) the ETL handles updates via SCD Type 1 overwrite or controlled backfill. Option B overstates the columnar compression advantage: a category_name column in a 100K-row dimension will compress well regardless of normalization. The join cost in BI engines — especially tools generating live SQL — often exceeds the marginal storage difference. Option C (ETL-enforced constraints) provides an integrity guarantee only if the ETL never makes a mistake, which is not a structural guarantee. It also adds ETL complexity without eliminating the physical update anomaly risk. Option D (OBT) is appropriate for single-table ML feature extraction or Presto-style full-table scans but abandons shared dimension reusability — every new fact that needs the product hierarchy must re-embed all product attributes, scaling the update anomaly problem by the number of facts.
hints: If 500 products share the 'Electronics' category and you rename that category, how many rows must be updated in a normalized three-table snowflake versus a denormalized single dimension table?
When is the update anomaly cost from denormalization acceptable? Consider how often category names change versus how often BI tools join through the product hierarchy to produce dashboards.

title: Data Vault Basics: Mapping a Kimball Customer Dimension to Vault Constructs
scenario_context: A team migrating from a Kimball star schema to a Data Vault 2.0 integration layer must map their existing `dim_customer` SCD Type 2 table to Data Vault constructs. The dimension currently has: customer_sk (system-generated surrogate), customer_id (natural key from the CRM), customer_email (contact identifier stored by the marketing system), customer_name, customer_tier, effective_from, effective_to. The team asks which Data Vault constructs replace the Kimball dimension and how each field maps.
description: What is the correct Data Vault mapping for `dim_customer`, and what advantage does separating CRM attributes from marketing attributes into distinct Satellites provide?
options: A Hub stores the CRM business key (customer_id); a Satellite for the CRM source holds customer_name and customer_tier with load_date and record_source; a second Satellite for the marketing source holds customer_email with its own load_date and record_source. Separating Satellites by source means a schema change in the marketing feed does not require modifying the CRM Satellite or the Hub.

A Hub stores both business keys (customer_id and customer_email) as a composite key. A single Satellite stores all descriptive attributes with load_date for historization. The composite key guarantees uniqueness across both source systems without a separate integration step.

A Hub stores the surrogate key (customer_sk) as the business key because it uniquely identifies the customer across all systems. Satellites store the natural keys alongside descriptive attributes. Surrogate keys are more stable than natural keys because they never change when source systems are updated.

The entire Kimball dimension maps to a Hub-Satellite pair where the Hub holds customer_id and the Satellite holds all remaining fields including effective_from and effective_to. The Data Vault retains the SCD logic inline to preserve the existing historization design.
explanation: Option A is correct. In Data Vault: a Hub stores one business key per business concept (the natural key that exists in the source system); Satellites store descriptive attributes with load_date and record_source for historization. When customer attributes come from two separate source systems (CRM, marketing), best practice is to put each source's attributes into a separate Satellite keyed by hub_hash_key + load_date. The benefit: a schema change in the marketing system's customer feed (new column added, column renamed) modifies only that Satellite — the CRM Satellite and the Hub remain unchanged, preserving integration stability. Option B is wrong: Hubs store one business key per business concept, not a composite of two systems' keys. If the marketing system later stops using email as a primary identifier, the composite Hub definition breaks. Note: if the marketing system maintained genuinely independent customer records not linked via customer_id, the correct Data Vault design would be a separate MarketingCustomer Hub joined to the CRM Hub via a Link table — but that complexity is not warranted when one golden-source integration key already exists across both systems. Option C is critically wrong: Hubs must store business keys (natural keys from source systems), never system-generated surrogate keys. Surrogate keys have no business meaning and cannot be used to integrate records across multiple source systems. Option D is wrong for two reasons: (1) `effective_from / effective_to` is Kimball valid-time logic; Data Vault uses `load_date` (database transaction time), which is different; mixing them creates bi-temporal ambiguity; (2) flattening all sources into one Satellite re-creates the source-coupling problem that Data Vault's multi-Satellite design is intended to prevent.
hints: Which part of a raw vault stores a business concept's natural identifier, and which part stores its descriptive attributes? What distinguishes a natural key from a system-generated surrogate?

If both CRM and marketing attributes are stored in a single Satellite and the marketing team adds a new column to their customer export, what must be changed in the raw vault to incorporate the new column?

title: Additive vs Semi-Additive vs Non-Additive: Classifying Measures by Aggregation Behavior
description: A retail analytics fact table has four measures: (1) units_sold — number of units sold per transaction; (2) inventory_on_hand — stock level at end of day; (3) gross_margin_pct — (revenue − cost) / revenue for the transaction; (4) discount_amount — the dollar discount applied to the transaction. Which classification is correct, and what does each classification imply about how a BI tool can safely aggregate the measure?
options: units_sold and discount_amount are fully additive — summing across all dimensions including date produces a correct total. inventory_on_hand is semi-additive — summing across locations on a given day is valid, but summing across dates double-counts stock held on multiple days. gross_margin_pct is non-additive — it is a ratio that must be recomputed from underlying revenue and cost components, not summed.

All four measures are fully additive because the fact table records one row per transaction and summing transaction-level rows always produces a correct total regardless of which dimension the aggregation crosses.

inventory_on_hand and gross_margin_pct are both non-additive because neither represents a count or amount tied to a discrete event. units_sold and discount_amount are additive because they are unit or monetary values attached to a transaction.

gross_margin_pct is semi-additive because it varies by product and day but is constant across date-only aggregations; inventory_on_hand is additive because summing stock across warehouses gives correct total company inventory.
explanation: Option A is the correct classification. Fully additive measures (units_sold, discount_amount) make mathematical sense when summed across any combination of dimensions — units sold in January plus units sold in February equals units sold in Q1. Semi-additive measures (inventory_on_hand) make sense summed across some dimensions (warehouse A on-hand plus warehouse B on-hand equals total company on-hand on a given day) but not across time (Monday on-hand plus Tuesday on-hand does not equal weekly on-hand — it double-counts stock held on both days). Semi-additive measures typically appear in periodic snapshot facts and require special time-dimension aggregation logic: LAST_VALUE, AVG, or MAX over the date axis, not SUM. Non-additive measures (gross_margin_pct) are ratios: summing percentages across rows produces a meaningless number. The correct aggregate is computed from the underlying additive components: SUM(revenue − cost) / SUM(revenue). Option B is wrong: inventory_on_hand in a daily snapshot fact is semi-additive even when the table has one row per snapshot per day — the issue is the semantics of summing across time, not the table structure. Option C is wrong: gross_margin_pct is non-additive (not semi-additive) and inventory_on_hand is semi-additive (not non-additive). Option D is wrong: gross_margin_pct is a ratio and is non-additive — no dimension combination makes SUM(gross_margin_pct) a correct metric.
hints: If today's warehouse holds 500 units and tomorrow holds 480 units, does 500 + 480 = 980 represent a meaningful inventory count? What does that tell you about summing inventory across the date dimension?
What SQL aggregate function gives the correct month-end inventory for a daily snapshot fact — SUM, AVG, or LAST_VALUE? What does that choice tell you about the measure's additivity?

title: Debug: Inflated Revenue When a Fact Joins a Many-Row Dimension
description: An analyst queries January revenue with this SQL: `SELECT SUM(f.revenue) FROM fact_orders f JOIN dim_promotion p ON f.order_key = p.order_key WHERE f.order_month = '2024-01'`. The result is $4.2M but Finance confirms the correct total is $2.1M. Investigation shows `dim_promotion` stores one row per promotion applied per order, and 60% of January orders had exactly two promotions applied. What is the root cause and the correct fix?
options: Root cause: `dim_promotion` is at the order-promotion level (one row per promotion per order), while `fact_orders` is at the order level (one row per order). The join multiplies each order's revenue by the number of promotions applied — orders with two promotions are counted twice. Fix: pre-aggregate `dim_promotion` to one row per order before joining, or redesign it as a bridge table with weights to distribute revenue across promotions.

Root cause: the WHERE clause `order_month = '2024-01'` excludes orders that span two months. Fix: change the filter to `order_month BETWEEN '2024-01' AND '2024-02'` and divide the revenue by 2 for orders that span the boundary.
Root cause: `fact_orders` contains duplicate order rows from an ETL bug. Fix: change SUM(f.revenue) to SUM(DISTINCT f.revenue) to collapse duplicate revenue values in the aggregation.
Root cause: `dim_promotion` joins on `order_key` but the fact table uses `order_id` internally; the key mismatch creates a Cartesian product. Fix: alias both columns to a shared name before joining.
explanation: Option A is correct. The fact table has one row per order; `dim_promotion` has one row per order-promotion combination. When fact_orders (order-level) joins to dim_promotion (order-promotion-level) on order_key, each order row is matched to as many promotion rows as it has promotions applied. For 60% of orders with exactly two promotions, each order's revenue is summed twice. This is the classic fan-out problem: a fact table joined to a dimension at a finer grain multiplies the fact row by the join cardinality. The fix is to either (1) pre-aggregate dim_promotion to one row per order with `SELECT DISTINCT order_key FROM dim_promotion` for revenue queries, or (2) redesign dim_promotion as a bridge table with a weight column (0.5 for two promotions) that sums to 1 per order so weighted revenue across promotions equals the original order revenue. Option B is wrong: the WHERE clause filter does not cause row multiplication; the inflated total is exactly 2×, which matches the 60% of orders each contributing 2 revenue rows. Option C is wrong: SUM(DISTINCT f.revenue) removes rows with the same revenue amount, not duplicate joins — it would incorrectly collapse different orders that happen to have the same revenue value. Option D is wrong: the problem statement uses `order_key` consistently; a key mismatch of this type would produce a Cartesian product of millions of rows, not a clean 2× inflation.
hints: If `dim_promotion` has one row per promotion per order and an order has two promotions, how many times does that order appear in the result of `fact_orders JOIN dim_promotion ON order_key`?

The total is exactly 2× the correct amount. Is this consistent with a Cartesian product (which would be much larger), a date-filter error, or each order's revenue being counted twice due to a join cardinality mismatch?

title: Schema from Requirements: Designing a Fact Table for a Multi-Dimension Brief
scenario_context: A stakeholder brief states: 'We need to analyze total sales revenue by customer, product, sales region, promotion, and date — and we need the ability to drill from quarterly revenue down to individual order lines.' The brief implies two analysis levels: executive dashboards aggregate to the order-header level (one row per order), while operations reports require line-item detail (one row per product per order). The team debates whether to build one fact table or two.
description: What is the correct level-of-detail decision and fact table structure, and why does trying to satisfy both analysis levels with a single fact table fail?
options: Build `fact_order_lines` at the order-line level (one row per product per order) with customer_key, product_key, region_key, promotion_key, date_key, line_revenue, and line_quantity. Executive dashboards aggregate line-level revenue with SUM — no precision is lost rolling up from fine to coarse. A separate order-header fact duplicates data and creates two sources of truth for the same revenue.

Build two separate facts: `fact_orders` at the order-header level for executive dashboards and `fact_order_lines` at the order-line level for operations. Each stakeholder queries only the appropriate fact; keeping levels separate prevents accidental double-counting when dashboards mix order-level and line-level metrics.

Build `fact_orders` at the order-header level and add an array or JSON column containing all line items inline. Executive dashboards query header columns; operations expand the array for line-level detail without a separate fact table.

Build one fact at the order-header level. For line-item detail, create a database view that unnests a summary column into pseudo-line rows. The view gives the appearance of line-level detail without storing one row per product per order.
explanation: Option A is correct: build at the finest level of detail required. Aggregate functions (SUM, COUNT) roll up correctly from fine to coarse — order-line revenue sums to order revenue, which sums to quarterly revenue. Information loss goes only one direction: a coarser-level fact cannot be disaggregated to finer detail. Since the brief explicitly requires order-line drill-down, the order-line level must be the physical fact level. Executive dashboards wanting order-level revenue simply apply GROUP BY order_key. This is the 'build at the finest level' principle in dimensional modeling. Option B (two separate facts) creates two revenue sources of truth: if `fact_orders.total_revenue` ever diverges from `SUM(fact_order_lines.line_revenue) GROUP BY order_key`, inconsistent reports appear. Separate facts for the same business process are justified only when the levels represent genuinely different business events (a purchase event vs. a return event). Option C (JSON array column) is incompatible with standard SQL GROUP BY, window functions, and BI tool query generation — most BI tools cannot filter or aggregate inside a JSON array without custom parsing. Option D (view over header fact) is circular: order-line detail cannot be recovered from an order-header total; the view would have to fabricate line data, not reconstruct it.
hints: If you have line-level revenue for each product on an order, can you always compute the order-header total? If you only have the order-header total, can you recover individual product revenues? What does this asymmetry suggest about which level to physically store?
Executive dashboards that need quarterly totals from line-level data use which SQL function? Is any accuracy lost in that aggregation compared to storing the totals directly?

title: Normalization vs Star Schema: Choosing the Right Design for a Reporting Data Mart
description: A data warehouse team chooses between a Third Normal Form (3NF) design and a Kimball star schema for a reporting data mart. The system will support: (1) 10 OLTP applications writing concurrent product updates, (2) executive dashboards generated by a BI tool via SQL, and (3) 50M new rows added to the main fact table daily. Which trade-off analysis correctly reflects when each design is appropriate?
options: 3NF minimizes update anomalies and storage for write-heavy workloads — correct for the 10 OLTP applications that need write consistency. A star schema denormalizes dimensions for query simplicity — correct for read-heavy BI dashboards where multi-table joins slow BI tool SQL generation. The standard pattern is a 3NF integration layer for operational writes and a star schema presentation layer for reporting.

3NF is always preferable; dashboards requiring simple queries should use materialized views over the 3NF tables rather than maintaining a separate denormalized reporting layer. Materialized views eliminate the performance gap without the update anomaly risk of denormalization.

A star schema is always preferable for any data warehouse scenario because columnar storage engines handle wide denormalized tables better than narrow normalized tables; nightly ETL rebuilds eliminate the update anomaly risk during the daily load window.

3NF and star schema have identical query performance in modern columnar warehouses because query optimizers automatically flatten join trees during execution planning; the choice is a governance preference with no runtime impact.
explanation: Option A is correct. The 3NF vs star schema question is about access pattern, not universal superiority. 3NF is optimized for write consistency: it eliminates update anomalies by storing each attribute exactly once, making concurrent OLTP writes correct and efficient. Star schema is optimized for read simplicity: dimension attributes are denormalized into a small number of wide tables so BI tools generate simple 2-table joins (fact + one dimension) rather than 8-table normalized joins. The standard enterprise architecture separates these concerns: a 3NF integration layer for operational writes and a star schema presentation layer for BI. Option B (always 3NF + materialized views) is defensible for some architectures but 'always' is wrong. Maintaining materialized views over a 3NF model with 50M daily rows requires complex incremental refresh logic that frequently underperforms a purpose-built dimensional mart. Option C (always star schema) fails for write-heavy OLTP applications: denormalized dimensions require updating all affected rows when an attribute changes — expensive and error-prone under 10 concurrent writers. Option D is empirically wrong: query optimizer join flattening has practical limits. Complex 8-way normalized joins consistently underperform equivalent 2-way star joins in production BI workloads across BigQuery, Redshift, and Snowflake.
hints: Reading a product hierarchy for a BI dashboard and updating a product attribute written by 10 concurrent applications are fundamentally different access patterns. Which design serves reads better, and which serves concurrent writes better?

If 50M daily rows reference a product attribute that is stored denormalized across the fact and dimension, how many rows must be updated when that attribute changes? How does this compare to updating one row in a normalized lookup table?

title: Debug: Revenue Double-Count from a Role-Playing Dimension Join
description: A BI analyst queries sales revenue by shipping region and billing region simultaneously: `SELECT ship.region_name AS ship_region, bill.region_name AS bill_region, SUM(f.revenue) FROM fact_sales f JOIN dim_geography ship ON f.ship_geo_key = ship.geo_key JOIN dim_geography bill ON f.bill_geo_key = bill.geo_key GROUP BY ship.region_name, bill.region_name`. The result shows $8.4M total revenue, but Finance confirms the correct total is $4.2M. What is the root cause?
options: The join is not the root cause. A role-playing join where the same dimension is aliased twice does not multiply rows when each fact row has exactly one ship_geo_key and one bill_geo_key — each key matches exactly one dimension row. The 2× inflation indicates duplicate rows in `fact_sales`. The analyst should verify with `SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT sale_id) FROM fact_sales`.

Root cause: a fan-out from an incorrect join — `fact_sales` has a many-to-many relationship with `dim_geography` because one region serves as both shipping and billing for different orders. Fix: add a filter `WHERE ship.geo_key != bill.geo_key` to exclude intra-region orders.

Root cause: SUM is applied before the GROUP BY, causing revenue to be counted once per region combination before being summed at the group level. Fix: use a subquery that SUM(revenue) per sale_id first, then join to geography aliases in the outer query.

Root cause: the two joins to `dim_geography` create a Cartesian product because the query engine cannot distinguish the two aliases of the same physical table. Fix: create two physical copies of `dim_geography` — one named `dim_shipping_geo` and one `dim_billing_geo` — and join each separately.
explanation: Option A is correct. A role-playing dimension join — where the same physical table is aliased twice under different names — does not produce row multiplication as long as each alias join key is unique per fact row. Each `fact_sales` row has exactly one `ship_geo_key` and one `bill_geo_key`; the two joins each match exactly one row from `dim_geography`, leaving the total row count unchanged. If the total revenue is exactly 2×, the root cause is duplicate sale rows in `fact_sales` — likely from an ETL load issue. Validating with `COUNT(*) vs COUNT(DISTINCT sale_id)` will confirm. Option B mischaracterizes role-playing joins: two join paths to the same physical dimension on different FK columns do not create a many-to-many relationship. Each FK is a single value; each join matches exactly one dimension row. The `WHERE ship.geo_key != bill.geo_key` filter would merely exclude orders where shipping and billing geographies are the same, not fix any double-counting. Option C misunderstands SQL semantics: SUM is always an aggregate applied after GROUP BY evaluation; this is not a mechanism that causes duplication. Option D is wrong: SQL query engines correctly handle multiple aliases of the same physical table — this is the standard role-playing dimension pattern and does not require physical copies of the dimension.
hints: If each row in `fact_sales` has exactly one ship_geo_key and one bill_geo_key, and each key matches exactly one row in `dim_geography`, how many times does each fact row appear after both joins are evaluated?

Total revenue is exactly 2× the correct amount. Is a 2× inflation consistent with a join Cartesian product (which would be much larger), or with a simpler explanation like each sale row appearing twice in the source table?

title: dbt Modeling Layers: Staging, Intermediate, and Mart Responsibilities for a Kimball Mart
scenario_context: A data team adopts dbt to build a Kimball-style dimensional mart for sales analytics. Their source is a Postgres OLTP database with tables: orders, order_items, customers, products, and regions. The delivery target is: dim_customer, dim_product, dim_geography, and fact_sales for a BI layer. A new data engineer asks how to assign work across staging (stg_), intermediate (int_), and mart (mart_) layers.
description: Which layer assignment correctly reflects the responsibility of each dbt modeling layer for this Kimball mart?
options: Staging (stg_orders, stg_customers, etc.): one-to-one with source tables — rename columns, cast types, deduplicate. No business logic, no cross-source joins. Intermediate (int_orders_with_items, int_customers_enriched): multi-source joins and business logic (compute LTV, join order header to lines). Mart (dim_customer, fact_sales): final dimensional shape with surrogate key generation, SCD logic, and declared level of detail. BI tools query only mart models.

Staging models handle all transformations from source to final dimensional shape in a single pass; intermediate and mart layers are optional for small teams and add unnecessary pipeline complexity. A single-layer approach reduces failure surface and accelerates delivery.

Intermediate models are the source-of-truth layer for all business logic; staging and mart models are formatting wrappers. Mart models should be thin views over intermediate models with no additional transformation beyond column renaming.

Mart models should include raw source columns alongside transformed columns so BI users can inspect original values and see where overrides were applied. Staging handles only type casting; intermediate is used only for multi-source unions.
explanation: Option A correctly describes the three-layer dbt pattern for Kimball work. Staging: one model per source table, light transformation only (rename, cast, dedup) — creates a stable, auditable interface over source systems with no business logic. Intermediate: where cross-source joins and business logic live (join order headers to lines, compute customer LTV, classify by tier) — pre-joined surfaces that the mart layer consumes cleanly. Mart: the dimensional output — surrogate key generation, SCD effective date logic, and the final column contract that BI tools see. This separation allows teams to change intermediate business logic without rebuilding staging, and to swap a source system (update staging) without rewriting business logic in the intermediate layer. Option B (all in staging) collapses when source systems change: any source modification forces a rebuild of all transformation logic embedded in one model. It also prevents reuse — the same enrichment must be duplicated if needed by two mart models. Option C (intermediate as SoT, mart as thin view) misplaces key responsibilities: surrogate key generation and SCD logic are dimensional modeling decisions that belong in the mart layer, not in intermediate models that may be reused across multiple marts with different SCD requirements. Option D (raw source columns in mart) exposes source volatility directly to BI consumers — if a source column is renamed, all downstream BI workbooks referencing the raw column break.
hints: If a staging model's output columns are queried directly by BI tools and a source system renames a column, which layer must be updated and how far does the change propagate?

Surrogate key generation and SCD date logic transform source data into a dimensional model artifact. Which layer — staging, intermediate, or mart — is the right home for this transformation, and why not earlier layers?

title: Grain Selection: Procedure vs Visit Level for a Hospital Analytics Fact
scenario_context: A hospital analytics team is designing a fact table for two requirements: (1) 'How many unique patients visited each department in Q3?' and (2) 'What was the total revenue from those visits?' The source operational system creates one row per patient per visit per procedure — a patient visiting cardiology for an EKG and a stress test generates two procedure rows under one visit. The team debates grain: procedure-level (one fact row per procedure per visit) vs visit-level (one fact row per visit).
description: Which level of detail correctly satisfies both requirements, and what does the wrong choice make impossible to answer later?
options: Use the procedure-level detail (one fact row per procedure per visit). Revenue per visit is summed from procedure rows; unique patient counts use COUNT(DISTINCT patient_key). Both requirements are answerable without information loss because procedure is the finest level available in the source and roll-up to visit or quarter is lossless.

Use the visit-level detail (one fact row per visit) and store total visit revenue as a pre-aggregated measure. Unique patient counts are a direct COUNT(patient_key). The procedure level is too fine for analytics — analysts need visit-level summaries, not procedure-level transactions.

Build two separate facts: `fact_visits` at the visit level for patient counts and `fact_procedures` at the procedure level for revenue detail. Executive dashboards query fact_visits; revenue drilldown queries fact_procedures. Keeping levels separate prevents COUNT(DISTINCT) queries that are slow at scale.

Use the visit-level fact and add a procedures JSON array column containing all procedure codes and amounts per visit. Revenue is computed by expanding the array; unique patient counts remain simple COUNTs.
explanation: Option A is correct. Building the fact at the finest available level preserves all analytical flexibility. Revenue sums from procedure rows; unique patient counts use COUNT(DISTINCT patient_key). Roll-up to visit, department, or quarter is always lossless via GROUP BY. Option B (visit-level with pre-aggregated revenue) breaks the moment the team needs revenue by procedure type (EKG, stress test, blood panel) — that detail cannot be reconstructed from a visit-level total. Pre-aggregated measures cannot be disaggregated. Option C (two separate facts) creates two sources of truth for revenue: if fact_visits.total_revenue ever diverges from SUM(fact_procedures.procedure_revenue) GROUP BY visit_key, reports conflict. Two facts for the same business process (a patient visit) are justified only when the levels represent genuinely different business events. Option D (JSON array on visit-level fact) is incompatible with standard SQL GROUP BY and BI tool query generation; most analytical engines cannot aggregate inside a JSON array without custom parsing logic, and the visit-level fact still cannot answer procedure-type revenue questions.
hints: If you store facts at the visit level and a report later asks for revenue by procedure type (EKG, stress test, blood draw), can you answer from a fact that only stores total visit revenue? What precision is permanently lost?

COUNT(DISTINCT patient_key) is standard SQL. At what row count does it typically become a performance bottleneck — thousands of visits, or hundreds of millions? Does the procedure level create that scale problem for a single hospital?

title: M1 Follow-up: Tracking Readmissions When the Business Rule Adds a New Event Relationship
scenario_context: Following M1: the hospital analytics team has built `fact_procedures` at the procedure-per-visit level. The clinical quality team adds a new requirement: 'Flag any patient who returns to the same department within 30 days of a prior visit as a readmission.' This requires linking two visits for the same patient and department. The team debates whether to add a readmission flag to `fact_procedures` or redesign the structure.
description: How does the readmission requirement change the fact design, and what is the minimum structural change that satisfies the requirement without creating a new source of truth for visit revenue?
options: Add a boolean `is_readmission` flag and a `prior_visit_key` foreign key to `fact_procedures`, populated at ETL time by checking each patient's prior visit history per department within a 30-day window. This is the minimum structural change: it adds derived attributes to the existing fact without altering its level of detail or creating a second revenue source.

Redesign the fact to the visit-pair level (one row per patient per consecutive visit pair) to explicitly model the readmission relationship as a first-class fact row with first_visit_key, readmission_visit_key, and days_between. This is the correct relational design for an event-to-event relationship.

Create a separate `fact_readmissions` table containing one row per readmission visit with patient_key, department_key, prior_visit_key, and days_since_prior. The original `fact_procedures` is unchanged; the readmission fact is joined when readmission metrics are needed.
Store a `readmission_count` on `dim_patient`, updated nightly. Reports filter `fact_procedures` for patients with dim_patient.readmission_count > 0. This avoids changing the fact table schema.
explanation: Option A is correct as the minimum structural change. Adding `is_readmission` and `prior_visit_key` at ETL time follows the derived attribute pattern: the ETL computes the flag from existing visit history and embeds it on the fact row. This enables readmission cohort filtering (WHERE is_readmission = TRUE) and drill-through to the prior visit (JOIN on prior_visit_key) without changing the fact's level of detail. Option B (visit-pair level) is a more principled design for dedicated readmission analysis, but it is not the minimum change — it requires a new fact table, a new level of detail, and a new ETL pipeline. If readmission is a secondary requirement layered on top of primary procedure analytics, Option A is the correct incremental evolution. Option C (separate readmission fact) creates two analytical surfaces for a property of an existing event. For a boolean attribute of a visit, an embedded flag on the existing fact is simpler and keeps the revenue source of truth unified. Option D (counter on dim_patient) violates the principle that derived metrics belong on facts, not dimensions. A dimension attribute should describe the customer's stable characteristics — a rolling 30-day behavioral metric is a transient fact property, not a stable customer attribute.
hints: Adding a boolean flag and a foreign key to an existing fact table changes its column count but not its row count or level of detail. What type of schema evolution is this — backwards-compatible or breaking?

If you create a separate readmission fact table, an analyst querying 'revenue from readmission visits' now needs to join two facts. What operational burden does this create compared to a flag on the existing fact?

title: Hierarchies: Mid-Year Product Reclassification in a Year-Spanning Revenue Report
scenario_context: A retailer's product hierarchy has Category (Electronics, Apparel) and Department (Consumer, Enterprise). In March, the product 'Tablet Pro X' is reclassified from Consumer to Enterprise while remaining in Electronics. The analytics team produces an annual revenue report by department. Under the current dim_product design, the Tablet Pro X shows all 12 months of revenue under Enterprise — including January and February when it was classified as Consumer. The difference is material: $240K is incorrectly attributed to Enterprise instead of Consumer for Q1.
description: What is the root cause of the reporting error, and what design change correctly reflects department membership at the time of each transaction?
options: Root cause: dim_product uses a Type 1 design that overwrites the department attribute on reclassification. Fix: apply SCD Type 2 to the department attribute on dim_product (effective_from / effective_to dates). fact_sales joins to the dimension row valid at the time of the transaction: pre-reclassification sales join to the Consumer row, post-reclassification sales join to the Enterprise row.

Root cause: the fact_sales table lacks a department_key column. Fix: add department_key directly to each fact row at load time, snapshotting the department at the time of the transaction and avoiding any dependence on how dim_product tracks historical department values.

Root cause: the product hierarchy has two levels above the product, which creates reclassification ambiguity. Fix: flatten category and department into a single classification code on dim_product to eliminate mid-year reclassification misattribution.

Root cause: the report spans the reclassification date. Fix: produce two sub-reports — one for January–February and one for March–December — and sum the department totals in the presentation layer. No schema change is required.
explanation: Option A is correct. The root cause is SCD Type 1 on dim_product: when the Tablet Pro X is reclassified in March, the existing dimension row is overwritten with department = Enterprise. All historical fact rows that previously joined to the Consumer row now resolve to Enterprise because the pointer (product_sk) is unchanged but the dimension row it points to has been updated. SCD Type 2 on the department attribute creates a new dimension row in March (new product_sk, effective_from = March 1, department = Enterprise), leaving the original row intact (effective_to = February 28, department = Consumer). fact_sales rows from January and February carry the old product_sk and join to the Consumer row; March and later carry the new product_sk and join to the Enterprise row. Option B also misidentifies the root cause: the problem is not that fact_sales lacks a department_key column — it is that dim_product's Type 1 design overwrites the historical department attribute, so every fact row that joins through product_sk now resolves to the post-reclassification department. More critically, Option B cannot retroactively correct the existing January-February rows without knowing what department_key to stamp on them; deriving that historical value requires exactly the version record that SCD Type 2 provides. As a forward-only change it also duplicates the classification between fact and dimension, increasing ETL maintenance burden whenever the department hierarchy changes. Option C (flatten hierarchy) does not solve the reclassification problem — a single classification code that changes mid-year has the same SCD challenge regardless of how many hierarchy levels exist. Option D (two sub-reports) is a manual workaround that fails with multiple reclassifications per year and cannot support ad hoc time-range queries.
hints: When a dimension attribute is overwritten on update and a fact row joins to the dimension using the stored dimension key, whose classification does the fact row now reflect — the classification at transaction time or the most recent classification?
Inserting a new dimension row when an attribute changes keeps the old row intact. What must fact rows from before the change reference for the historical classification to survive the update?

title: Surrogate vs Natural Keys: Why Dimensional Models Use Generated Keys Even When Source IDs Are Stable
description: A dimensional model team debates whether to use the source system's customer UUID (stable since 2018) as the dimension's primary key, or to generate an integer surrogate key. The source team argues: 'Our UUIDs are globally unique and never reused — there is no technical reason for an extra key.' What is the strongest justification for a generated key even when the source natural key is stable?
options: A generated key decouples the dimension from the source key scheme: if two source systems are merged and both use separate UUID spaces for the same business entity, the dimension can assign one unified key per canonical customer without requiring source UUIDs to match. SCD Type 2 also requires distinct keys: two dimension rows for the same customer at different time periods must have different keys so fact rows can point to the correct historical version.

Generated integer keys join faster than UUIDs because integer comparison requires fewer CPU cycles and integer columns compress better in columnar storage than 36-character strings. The performance benefit at scale justifies the additional ETL step.

Source natural keys are never truly stable — the UUID scheme could change in a future system re-platform. A generated key is insurance against future key instability, even if the source has been stable for six years.

Generated keys are a required Kimball compliance rule: any dimensional model that uses natural keys as dimension primary keys is non-compliant with the methodology regardless of source system key stability.
explanation: Option A gives the strongest justification with two concrete technical reasons. (1) Source system isolation: if two CRM systems are merged, each with separate UUID spaces for the same physical customer, the dimensional model assigns one generated key per canonical customer. All historical facts from both systems point to the unified key without requiring any source UUID to match or any fact-row updates. (2) SCD Type 2: when a customer's tier changes from Silver to Gold, two dimension rows exist with the same UUID but different generated keys. Fact rows before the change point to the pre-change generated key (Silver); fact rows after point to the post-change generated key (Gold). Without distinct generated keys, SCD Type 2 cannot function — the natural key alone cannot distinguish historical versions. Option B (performance) is partially valid but secondary: modern columnar engines handle UUID joins efficiently; performance is a benefit, not the primary justification. Option C (future instability) is speculative and weaker than Option A's concrete present-day cases. Option D is wrong: Kimball recommends generated keys for specific technical reasons — it is not a compliance rule for its own sake. A model that uses natural keys where technically appropriate is not 'non-compliant.'
hints: A company merges two CRM systems that assign different UUIDs to the same physical customer. How does the dimensional model unify 'Jane Smith' from both systems into one customer identity for cross-system revenue reporting?

SCD Type 2 creates two rows for the same customer when an attribute changes. If both rows share the same UUID as their primary key, how does a fact row from before the change reference the pre-change attribute values rather than the post-change values?

title: Pre-Aggregated Summary Tables: When They Help and When They Introduce Calculation Errors
scenario_context: A retail analytics team pre-builds a monthly summary table `agg_monthly_sales` (one row per product × month) with columns: total_units, total_revenue, avg_selling_price (= total_revenue / total_units computed at month-end). A new analyst uses this table to compute annual revenue per product as SUM(total_revenue) and annual average selling price as SUM(avg_selling_price). Revenue totals match Finance's source reports exactly, but average selling price is wrong by up to 40% for some products.
description: What is the root cause of the average selling price error, and what is the correct computation from the monthly summary table?
options: avg_selling_price is non-additive: it is a ratio (total_revenue / total_units) pre-computed per month. SUM(avg_selling_price) produces a simple sum of monthly ratios — not a weighted average — which is wrong when monthly unit volumes differ. The correct annual average selling price is SUM(total_revenue) / SUM(total_units), recomputed from the underlying additive components.

avg_selling_price is semi-additive: it can be averaged across months but not summed. The correct computation is AVG(avg_selling_price) across months, which weights all months equally and produces the correct annual average.

The summary table is the wrong data source for annual averages; the analyst must query the underlying transaction-level fact table and compute AVG(selling_price) directly, since pre-aggregated ratios always lose the precision needed for annual metrics.
avg_selling_price should be stored as a cumulative running total in `agg_monthly_sales` rather than a monthly average. SUM() across the cumulative column would then produce the correct annual figure.
explanation: Option A is correct. avg_selling_price is non-additive: it is a ratio pre-computed within each month. SUM of ratios is not the ratio of sums. Consider a product with 1000 units at avg $10 in January and 10 units at avg $100 in February: the correct annual average is (10000 + 1000) / (1010) = $10.89. SUM(10, 100) = $110 — wrong by nearly 10×. AVG(10, 100) = $55 — still wrong because it weights the low-volume February equally with the high-volume January. The correct computation from the summary table is SUM(total_revenue) / SUM(total_units) = 11000 / 1010 = $10.89, using the additive components that were preserved in the summary table. Option B (AVG) is wrong: AVG weights each month equally regardless of unit volume, producing an unweighted average that is incorrect when monthly volumes differ significantly. Option C (use transaction-level fact) is correct in principle but impractical — it defeats the purpose of the pre-aggregated table. The summary table already contains the additive components (total_units, total_revenue) needed to reconstruct a correct weighted average. Option D (cumulative storage) is not meaningful: storing a running cumulative ratio destroys the ability to compute any sub-annual or partial-period metric from the summary table.
hints: A product sells 1000 units in January at avg $10 and 10 units in February at avg $100. SUM(10, 100) = $110 and AVG(10, 100) = $55 as annual averages. What is the correct annual average — and which computation with the columns available in the summary table produces it?

total_revenue and total_units are fully additive measures in the summary table. Is avg_selling_price = total_revenue / total_units additive in the same way? What happens mathematically when you sum or average pre-computed ratios instead of recomputing the ratio from sums?

title: Debug: Orphaned Fact Rows After a Dimension Cleanup Deletes Referenced Rows
scenario_context: A data team 'cleans up' `dim_product` by deleting rows for any product discontinued before 2023. After the deletion, a revenue report shows $3.2M total, but the pre-cleanup total was $4.8M. The missing $1.6M represents sales from 2020–2022 that referenced products now deleted from the dimension. Analysts can no longer break down the $1.6M by product or category because those dimension rows no longer exist.
description: What went wrong and what is the correct pattern for handling inactive or discontinued entities in a dimensional model?
options: Root cause: the dimension deletion orphaned historical fact rows — their product_sk now has no matching dimension row, so the revenue from those rows is excluded from any JOIN-based revenue query. Fix: never delete dimension rows that have referencing fact rows; instead, mark discontinued products with an `is_active = FALSE` flag. Historical revenue queries include all rows; current-state filters add `WHERE is_active = TRUE`.

Root cause: the fact table lacks a foreign key constraint between fact_sales.product_sk and dim_product.product_sk. Fix: add an enforced foreign key constraint so the database engine prevents dimension row deletions that would orphan fact rows, raising an integrity error before any deletion completes.

Root cause: discontinued products should have been moved to a `dim_product_archive` table before deletion. Fix: rebuild dim_product_archive from the deleted rows (if possible from backup), and modify all revenue queries to UNION dim_product and dim_product_archive in the dimension join.

Root cause: the fact table stores product_sk (surrogate key) instead of product_id (natural key). Fix: migrate fact_sales to use product_id so the join survives dimension row deletions — if the product is later re-inserted with the same natural key, fact rows automatically rejoin.
explanation: Option A is correct. In a dimensional model, dimension rows should never be deleted while fact rows reference them. Every historical transaction must remain analytically addressable, including transactions from products that are now discontinued. The correct pattern is to mark inactive entities with a flag (is_active, is_discontinued, status = 'inactive') via SCD Type 1 overwrite. This gives two capabilities simultaneously: historical reports include all rows (no WHERE filter on is_active); current-state dashboards add WHERE is_active = TRUE to show only active products. Option B (foreign key constraint) is a valid database-level safeguard but not available in most analytical data warehouses (BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift do not enforce referential integrity). The correct primary remedy is the ETL practice of never deleting referenced dimension rows. Option C (archive table + UNION) creates two dimension surfaces for the same business concept, requiring all consumers to modify their JOIN logic. This is high operational overhead for a problem solved by a single boolean flag. Option D (natural key in fact) would prevent orphaning from deletions only if products are re-inserted with the same natural key — but it undermines SCD Type 2 (which requires different surrogate keys for different historical versions) and exposes facts to source system key changes.
hints: A 2021 fact row references a product discontinued in 2022 via its dimension key. After the dimension row is deleted, what does a SQL JOIN between fact_sales and dim_product return for that 2021 row?

An is_active flag on the dimension achieves two things simultaneously that deletion prevents: it excludes the product from current-state queries while still allowing historical revenue queries to resolve the join. Why does deletion prevent both?

title: Periodic Snapshot Facts: Why Account Balances Cannot Be Summed Across Days
scenario_context: A bank's analytics team needs to report account balance trends. The source system produces one row per transaction. The team debates: (A) a transaction-level fact where balance is computed as a running SUM of transactions, or (B) a daily periodic snapshot with each account's end-of-day balance. The VP of Analytics requires: 'I need to answer, on any given day, the total balance held across all accounts — instantly, not via a multi-minute window function scan.'
description: Which fact design correctly supports the VP's query requirement, and why does the transaction-level approach fail for this specific query pattern?
options: Use a daily periodic snapshot (one row per account × day) with end-of-day balance as a stored measure. The VP's query is `SELECT SUM(balance) WHERE snapshot_date = target_date` — a simple aggregate on a single partition with no window function. Balance is additive across accounts on a given day but semi-additive across days: summing balances across 30 days would count each account's balance 30 times.

Use a transaction-level fact with each deposit and withdrawal. Compute balance via a window function: `SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY account_key ORDER BY transaction_date ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)`. This gives balance at any point in time and is more analytically flexible than a periodic snapshot.

Use a transaction-level fact and a separate balance ledger table updated nightly. The transaction fact handles transaction analytics; the ledger handles balance queries. Two separate tables serve two analytical needs without compromise.
Both designs are equivalent for the VP's query. A transaction-level fact with a window function computes balance as accurately as a periodic snapshot; the choice is purely about storage cost.
explanation: Option A is correct. The VP's question — 'total balance on a given day' — is a point-in-time state query, not an event aggregation. A daily periodic snapshot stores each account's end-of-day balance explicitly; the query is a simple SUM on a single date's rows. The critical property to understand: balance is semi-additive — it can be summed across accounts on a given day (warehouse A balance + warehouse B balance = total balance on that day) but not across time (Monday balance + Tuesday balance would count assets held on both days twice). Option B (transaction-level window function) requires a full unbounded window scan for every balance query — expensive at scale. BI tools also cannot generate `ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING` syntax from visual query builders; analysts must write raw SQL. Option C (transaction fact + separate ledger) introduces two revenue sources of truth for balance: if the nightly ledger job fails, the ledger and the transaction-computed balance diverge. Option D is empirically wrong: window functions on hundreds of millions of transaction rows are significantly more expensive than a pre-materialized periodic snapshot.
hints: The VP wants 'total balance on a given day' — is this a question about events that happened (deposits, withdrawals) or about state at a point in time (what was the balance on that date)? Which fact type is built for point-in-time state?

If daily balance is stored in a snapshot, SUM(balance) on a single snapshot_date gives today's total balance. What does SUM(balance) across all snapshot_dates in a month give — and why is that the wrong answer for 'total balance on March 15'?

title: M2 Follow-up: Computing Quarter-End Balance From a Daily Snapshot When the Business Rule Changes
scenario_context: Following M2: the bank's `fact_balance_snapshot` stores one row per account per day with end-of-day balance. The VP of Finance now requires 'quarter-end balance' — the total balance across all accounts as of the last business day of each quarter — for a regulatory filing. The current daily snapshot covers 5 years of daily data.
description: Can the daily snapshot satisfy this new requirement without a schema change, and what is the correct aggregation?
options: Yes — query the daily snapshot filtered to the last business day of each quarter (identifiable via a date dimension with is_quarter_end and is_business_day flags). `SELECT SUM(balance) WHERE snapshot_date = quarter_end_date` produces the correct quarter-end total balance. No schema change is needed; the daily snapshot already contains every quarter-end day's snapshot as a subset of its daily rows.

No — the daily snapshot must be redesigned as a quarterly snapshot (one row per account per quarter). A daily snapshot wastes storage for quarterly reporting and computing balance from daily rows incorrectly applies daily additivity to a quarterly aggregate.

Yes — compute quarterly balance as `AVG(balance) WHERE quarter = target_quarter` for each account, then sum. Averaging the daily balance across the quarter gives the correct 'representative' balance the VP intends by 'quarter-end.'

No — the query planner cannot determine the last business day of a quarter from the snapshot alone without a calendar table. A quarterly snapshot fact must be added alongside the daily snapshot to make quarter-end queries self-contained.
explanation: Option A is correct. The daily snapshot contains every calendar day, including the last business day of each quarter. The query `SELECT SUM(balance) FROM fact_balance_snapshot WHERE snapshot_date = [last business day of Q]` is semantically identical to the VP's requirement. A date dimension with is_quarter_end = TRUE and is_business_day = TRUE flags makes identifying the target date a simple join — this is standard practice in any dimensional model with a dim_date table. No schema change is needed; the daily snapshot is a superset of any coarser-period snapshot. Option B (redesign as quarterly) is unnecessary over-engineering: discarding the daily snapshot would prevent any daily, weekly, or intra-quarter balance analysis. The VP's new requirement adds a query pattern, not a new data requirement. Option C (AVG) is semantically wrong: 'quarter-end balance' is a point-in-time value, not an average. AVG(daily_balance) is average daily balance — a valid metric for interest calculations, but not what the VP asked for. Option D is wrong: identifying the last business day of a quarter is solved by a date dimension join, not by adding a new physical fact table. The requirement to answer a quarter-end query does not require storing a separate quarterly snapshot when the daily snapshot already contains the target date.
hints: The last business day of Q1 is a specific calendar date. If the daily snapshot has a row for that date for every account, what SQL expression retrieves the total balance across all accounts on exactly that date?

'Quarter-end balance' is a point-in-time balance value. Is this the same metric as 'average daily balance for the quarter'? Which SQL aggregate captures a point-in-time value from a set of daily snapshot rows?

title: Distinct-Count Metrics in Summary Tables: Why They Cannot Be Summed Across Time
scenario_context: A SaaS analytics team pre-builds a daily summary `agg_daily_active_users` (one row per product × day) with a `daily_active_users` column computed as COUNT(DISTINCT user_id). A product manager asks for monthly active users (MAU) — unique users active at any point in a month. A new analyst computes MAU as `SUM(daily_active_users) WHERE month = target_month`. The result is 5–8× the known MAU figure from the BI team.
description: What is the root cause of the over-count, and what is the correct approach for computing MAU from the available data?
options: COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) is non-additive across time: a user active on 20 days in a month is counted once in each day's COUNT(DISTINCT), so SUM across 30 days counts that user 20 times but MAU should count them once. Correct MAU requires either a transaction-level COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) over the month or a dedicated monthly pre-aggregated table.

SUM(daily_active_users) is correct for MAU when users can be active on multiple days; the result represents total user-days, not unique users. The BI team's lower number undercounts users who were active on multiple days.

The daily summary double-counts users active in both the morning and evening on a given day. The fix is to compute daily_active_users with a session-deduplicated COUNT rather than a raw COUNT(DISTINCT user_id).
MAU from the daily summary is MAX(daily_active_users) across the month — the peak unique user count on any single day, which represents the month's maximum unique user engagement.
explanation: Option A is correct. COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) is a non-additive measure across the time dimension because the same user entity is counted on each day they are active. A user active on 20 days contributes 1 to each day's COUNT(DISTINCT) but should contribute 1 to the monthly MAU. SUM(daily_active_users) gives total user-days — a distinct metric from unique monthly users. The correct computation for MAU is COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) over all activity records in the target month from the transaction-level fact, or a pre-computed monthly snapshot that runs the distinct count at aggregation time from the granular data. Option B confuses user-days (total engagement volume) with monthly active users (unique user count) — these are different metrics with different meanings. The analyst's number is wrong; the BI team's is correct. Option C is incorrect: COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) already handles multiple events per user per day — it counts each unique user exactly once per day regardless of event frequency. Option D (MAX) gives the peak single-day count, not the count of unique users across the month. A month with 2000 unique users but a single-day peak of 800 would show 800 — a significant undercount.
hints: If User A is active on 20 days in January, how many times does User A contribute to SUM(daily_active_users) across those 20 days? How many times should User A appear in January's count of unique monthly active users?

COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) on a single day counts each user once. Is the monthly COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) equal to the sum of 31 daily COUNT(DISTINCT) values? Under what condition would the two be equal, and does that condition hold for most real products?

title: Data Vault Schema Evolution: Adding Attributes from a New Source Without Polluting Existing Satellites
description: A Data Vault raw vault has `hub_customer` and a single satellite `sat_customer_crm` (customer_name, customer_tier from the CRM). A marketing platform is onboarded and provides additional customer attributes: preferred_channel, campaign_group, opt_in_email. The team debates: (A) add the three new columns to `sat_customer_crm` with NULL when marketing data is unavailable, or (B) create a new `sat_customer_marketing` containing only the marketing attributes. Which is correct and why?
options: Create `sat_customer_marketing` (customer_hash_key, load_date, record_source, preferred_channel, campaign_group, opt_in_email). Each satellite should be loaded from exactly one record source; mixing CRM and marketing attributes in one satellite couples two ETL pipelines into one table, so a marketing platform schema change forces a rebuild of the CRM satellite.

Add the three marketing columns to `sat_customer_crm` with nullable values. When marketing data is unavailable, columns stay NULL. This avoids proliferating narrow satellites and keeps all customer attributes together for simpler downstream joins.

Create a bridge table between the CRM satellite and a new marketing satellite to store cross-source customer attributes. The bridge resolves the many-to-one relationship between a customer and their marketing profile.

Add the marketing attributes to `hub_customer` as additional business key columns since preferred_channel and campaign_group are customer-identifying attributes used by the marketing team as their primary reference.
explanation: Option A is correct. The foundational satellite design rule is one satellite per record source. Each satellite's record_source column tracks which system provided the data; each satellite's load_date records when that system's load occurred. Mixing CRM and marketing attributes in one satellite creates two problems: (1) a load failure in the marketing ETL pipeline could delay CRM attribute loads that share the satellite's processing; (2) a schema change in the marketing platform (new column added) requires modifying sat_customer_crm, which is conceptually owned by the CRM team and may require their ETL to change. Separate satellites provide source isolation: marketing failures affect only sat_customer_marketing; the CRM satellite continues unaffected. Option B violates source isolation: NULLs in marketing columns create ambiguity — does NULL mean 'customer not in marketing system' or 'marketing ETL failed this run'? Separate satellites resolve the ambiguity by the presence or absence of the satellite row itself. Option C (bridge table) is the correct construct for Hub-to-Hub relationships, not for adding attributes from a second source to an existing business entity. A marketing attribute is a property of the customer entity, not a relationship between two entities. Option D is wrong: hub_customer stores business keys — natural identifiers used to uniquely identify a customer. preferred_channel is a marketing attribute, not an identifier; adding it to the Hub redefines what 'customer' means as a business key.
hints: The record_source column in a satellite records which system provided the data for each row. If CRM and marketing attributes share a satellite, what does record_source contain when a row has both CRM and marketing data populated simultaneously?

If the marketing platform changes its schema and adds a new customer segment column, which physical satellite table must be altered in each design — a shared satellite or a dedicated one? Which change is lower operational risk for the CRM team?

title: Debug: Historical Report Labels Change After a Dimension Attribute Is Overwritten
description: An analyst runs a monthly revenue report in October showing $2.4M under product tier 'Premium.' In November, after the ETL team renames the product tier from 'Premium' to 'Premium Plus' in `dim_product`, the October report now shows $2.4M under 'Premium Plus' — the revenue is correct but the label is wrong. The analyst confirms: no fact data changed, only the dimension row. What is the root cause and the correct fix?
options: Root cause: `dim_product` uses SCD Type 1 — the tier attribute is overwritten in place on rename. Historical fact rows still join to the same product_sk, which now resolves to 'Premium Plus.' The October label changed because the dimension row it references changed. Fix: use SCD Type 2 for tier — insert a new dimension row on rename (tier = 'Premium Plus', new effective_from) and retain the old row (tier = 'Premium', old effective_to), so historical fact rows continue to reference the pre-rename version.

Root cause: the fact table stores product_name as a VARCHAR column copied from the source rather than a foreign key to dim_product. Fix: replace the VARCHAR tier column in the fact with a product_sk foreign key. Fact rows would then join to the dimension rather than storing the label directly.

Root cause: the ETL team renamed the tier in the source operational system, which propagated to dim_product. Fix: block all dimension attribute changes from propagating to the warehouse once a value has been published; dimension attributes should be immutable after initial load.

Root cause: the BI tool caches the October report using stale dimension join values from before the rename. Fix: clear the BI tool's report cache after any dimension update to force a fresh join to current dimension attribute values.
explanation: Option A is correct. SCD Type 1 overwrites dimension attributes in place — it is explicitly designed so that a dimension update changes what all historical fact rows resolve to. The product_sk in historical October fact rows is unchanged, but the row it points to now says 'Premium Plus.' This is not a bug in SCD Type 1 — it is its intended behavior: 'always show current state.' If the requirement is 'show the tier name that was in effect at the time of the transaction,' SCD Type 2 is required. With SCD Type 2, renaming the tier creates a new product_sk row (tier = 'Premium Plus', effective_from = rename date); the old row (tier = 'Premium') retains its effective_to and is still referenced by October fact rows that carry the old product_sk. Option B is wrong: the fact table already stores product_sk as a foreign key — that is exactly the mechanism by which the renamed dimension attribute propagates to historical reports. The issue is the SCD strategy, not the key design. Option C (immutable dimensions) is operationally impossible for attributes that legitimately need correction or rebranding. The correct design decision is choosing the SCD type based on the business requirement. Option D (cache clearing) is wrong: the change is not a caching artifact. After clearing the cache, the October report would still show 'Premium Plus' because the dimension join returns the current, post-rename attribute value.
hints: When a dimension attribute is overwritten in place and a fact row joins to that dimension using a stored dimension key, whose attribute value does the fact row now reflect — the value at the time of the transaction, or the current value?
Which SCD type preserves historical attribute values by inserting a new dimension row for each attribute change, while retaining the old row with a bounded validity window?

title: Multiple Hierarchies: When Finance and Operations Define Product Categories Differently
scenario_context: A manufacturing company has two product hierarchy paths for the same SKUs: (1) Finance hierarchy — SKU → cost_center → business_unit; (2) Operations hierarchy — SKU → assembly_line → plant. The same Widget X belongs to cost_center 'R&D' in Finance and to assembly_line 'Line A, Plant 1' in Operations. Both Finance and Operations analysts query the same `fact_production` table and need to group revenue by their respective hierarchy paths.
description: What is the correct design for a product dimension that must serve two independent, non-overlapping hierarchy paths, and what does each alternative imply for query complexity or governance?
options: Add both hierarchy paths to a single `dim_product` row: cost_center_key, business_unit_key (Finance path) alongside assembly_line_key, plant_key (Operations path). A single product_sk is shared across both paths; fact_production joins once to dim_product regardless of which hierarchy is being navigated. Finance queries group by cost_center_key; Operations queries group by assembly_line_key.

Create two separate dimension tables: `dim_product_finance` (SKU + Finance hierarchy) and `dim_product_operations` (SKU + Operations hierarchy). Finance analysts join fact_production to dim_product_finance; Operations analysts join to dim_product_operations. Each dimension is maintained by the owning team.
